landingV2.welcome_subtitle: Coding lover and problem solver, building solutions that make hard tasks easier and automating the easy ones.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.closing_note: Thanks for reading this far. This page, like the rest of the site, is a work in progress that I keep refining as I learn, so if any part of it caught your interest the repository is the best place to dig in, and I am always happy to talk it through.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.sections.over: This site is my personal portfolio, and it doubles as the project I use to learn and to show how I build software. It is an Angular application split into several micro-frontends inside an Nx monorepo, where a shell app owns the router and mounts the rest at runtime. I wanted a real, non-trivial system to build rather than a single static page, something I could keep growing and improving over time.

The portfolio started as a way to learn, and it grew into the place where I try things out properly before using them elsewhere. I had several small ideas I wanted to ship as independent apps, so a monorepo that could build, test and deploy each one on its own fit the goal better than a single bundle.

Nx gave me that structure along with a real push to build small, focused libraries. As the project grew, keeping features and shared pieces in their own libraries kept everything easy to find, reason about and reuse, which matters more the larger it gets.
The shell is the only host. Every other app is a remote it composes at runtime, so the site is one experience made of parts that each stand on their own.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.sections.micr: The honest reason is learning. Micro-frontends and Module Federation are still new and not widely used, so building a real one taught me far more than reading about them would, and it lets me show that I can design and ship an architecture like this.

There are practical upsides too. Moving between apps never reloads Angular or the shared libraries, shared configuration lives in one place, and routing the locale first works across every app. None of that was strictly necessary for a portfolio, which is exactly why it was worth building and being able to explain.

I did not pick micro-frontends because a portfolio needs them. I picked them because I wanted to understand the model in depth: how a host composes remotes, how they share dependencies, and where the sharp edges are. Building one is the only way I have found to really learn that.

It also works as a demonstration. The architecture is more than a personal site needs, and that is deliberate. It shows I can reason about runtime composition, shared singletons and cross-app state rather than only wiring up components.

The practical wins are real even so. Because the shell and the shared libraries load once, moving between apps is cheap, global configuration is defined a single time, and the whole site can present one consistent, localized frame around independent pieces.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.sections.mf-t: The shell is the only host. It declares the remotes and lazy-loads each one's routes through a path alias like landingV2/Routes, so from the shell's point of view a remote's routes import like any local module even though they are served separately.

Each remote is built to run inside the shell, not on its own. Open a remote on its own port and you get a blank page by design: it bootstraps an empty entry component with no router outlet, so the router matches routes but has nothing to render into. The shell provides the outlet, the global styles and the locale context, so a remote only renders the way it will in production when the shell composes it.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.sections.loca: Every app can localize itself, and it runs through RokuTranslator, a small i18next wrapper I built by hand instead of pulling in a general library. It is a framework agnostic singleton shared across the whole federation, so the shell configures localization once and every app reads the same language and namespaces.

Each library registers its own translation namespace with per-locale lazy loaders, and switching language at runtime needs no rebuild. Locale-first routing is one part of this: the language is the first URL segment, which keeps pages shareable and cacheable per language.

I tried Transloco, plain i18next and a few other options, and none of them fit the shape I wanted, where each app owns its own locales and some apps might not localize at all. So I spent a while on a different approach and landed on a thin wrapper around i18next that reuses its key resolution and namespacing while isolating each library's translations.

It has two layers. RokuTranslator itself is a framework agnostic singleton that holds the active locale and the registered namespaces. On top sits an Angular adapter, provided per library, that registers what that library needs and keeps it scoped to its own namespace. The singleton exists because only the shell can run an app initializer, so localization is configured once there and shared everywhere.

Remotes contribute their own translations through per-locale lazy loaders, a small custom i18next backend, so a remote can register its language files at runtime without the shell knowing about them upfront. In the Module Federation config the wrapper is forced to a strict singleton, which is what stops the active locale from fragmenting so two apps can never show different languages at once.

Locale-first routing sits on top. The first URL segment is the language, and a pair of route guards resolve the intended locale on entry and rewrite the URL when it drifts, so a stale segment never fights the active language.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.sections.orga: Almost everything lives in libraries, not in the apps. The apps stay thin: they wire things together and little else. The libraries are grouped by scope and by kind, feature libraries, ui, data-access and models, so it is clear what each piece is and where it belongs.

Most code starts inside a shared ui or utils library. Something graduates to a library of its own mainly when it has grown into a real feature in its own right and gains value from being independent, revised and reused on its own terms.

The default home for new code is a library. Within a scope I follow Nx's conventions: data-access for services, feature libraries for routed features, ui for presentational components, and models for types. The apps themselves hold almost no logic, which keeps them easy to reason about and makes the libraries the real substance of the project.

Deciding when something deserves its own library comes down to whether it is a genuine feature or broadly reusable. Small components and helpers stay inside an existing library. Something earns its own library when it outgrows the shared ui or utils library and stands on its own, especially when it has nothing to do with the interface and does not depend on Angular.

RokuTranslator is the clearest example. I use it across every app and gave it its own libraries because I revise it often and did not want something that changes that much destabilising the shared code. The rule for shared code is that it must be usable without much configuration; when it is not, I keep two focused components and extract the common piece rather than ship one component buried in options. Everything crosses a library boundary through its path alias, never a relative path.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.sections.asse: Assets live with the libraries that use them. Each library keeps its own assets, its translation files, icons and images, next to the code that needs them rather than in one global folder, so a library stays self-contained and easy to move or reuse.

When an app is built, its assets are bundled with it; the workspace is configured so each app collects the assets from the libraries it depends on. Icons are handled in code rather than as loose files: each SVG is imported as a raw string and inlined through Angular's sanitizer as a small standalone component, so icons ship as part of the bundle and stay easy to reuse.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.sections.infr: The project lives on GitHub, and GitHub Actions runs the pipeline. On every push it works out which projects were actually affected and only lints, tests and builds those, which keeps CI fast as the workspace grows.
Each app is containerized with Docker and deployed to a small Kubernetes cluster with Helm. Changes flow through a staging environment first and then to production on a tagged release.
Tests run at two levels: Jest for unit tests and Cypress or Playwright for end to end. The end-to-end tests all point at the shell, because the shell is how the apps are actually used.

CI runs on GitHub Actions and leans on Nx's affected detection: it compares against the last successful run and only builds and tests the projects that changed, so the pipeline stays quick even as the number of apps and libraries grows.

Images are built by a custom Nx plugin I wrote, @portfolio/docker, which wraps docker buildx with build and push executors plus a small generator for scaffolding a new app's Dockerfile. Each Angular app builds to static files served behind a reverse proxy, and the images are environment agnostic apart from the shell, which embeds its micro-frontend base URL at build time.

Deployment targets a k3s cluster through a single Helm release. A push to the main branch builds the affected apps and rolls them out to staging, and publishing a release builds everything at that commit and pins it to production, so production always runs immutable, versioned images and a rollback is just redeploying an older version.
landingV2.detail.portfolio.sections.test: The data-access layer uses a shared-spec pattern. I know the types each service must return, so I wrote one contract suite that every implementation of that service has to pass. Each concrete implementation runs the shared suite first and then adds its own tests, so every version is held to the same behavior on top of its specific cases.

End-to-end tests are organized per app but always point at the shell rather than a remote's own port, because the shell is how a real user reaches each app. It is an area I am still refining, especially for micro-frontends, but pointing e2e at the shell keeps the tests honest about how the site actually runs.
landingV2.detail.odontogram.what_body: A full odontogram for recording dental treatments and keeping each patient's history over time.
landingV2.detail.odontogram.hard_part_bo: A tooth has up to six zones, and a single treatment can affect several zones and span more than one tooth. The SVG chart maps every click back to the right zone and tooth, and persists the resulting state.
landingV2.detail.damocles.studio_body: A VR game studio founded by a group of university students who decided to build their own games using a technology that is still not standardized: virtual reality. Alongside their own titles, the studio also offers VR and gamification services to other companies.
landingV2.detail.damocles.work_body: STARLIT: ASCENSION, a VR shooter currently under development, sits alongside client R&D work such as Realistic Interactor and the VR Sickness Reducer, a graduated-exposure test built to reduce VR-induced dizziness.
landingV2.detail.damocles.built_body: An Angular micro-frontend with Home, About, Services and Contact pages sharing a component system translated into English, Spanish and French, a reactive contact form, and a data-access layer for news and projects.
